summary: Defines a RADIUS Attributes suboption that lets a network element pass identification and authorization attributes it got during RADIUS authentication to a DHCP server through the relay agent information option.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4014 defines a small addition to DHCP. When a switch or wireless access point checks a user's identity with RADIUS, the answer it gets back carries rules about what that user is allowed to do, such as which address pool to use. This document lets the access device pass those rules on to the DHCP server, inside a suboption of the relay agent information option, so that the DHCP server can choose the client's address accordingly.

subtitle: How a network access device hands RADIUS authorization attributes to a DHCP server through the relay agent.

tldr.problem: When a network access server authenticated a user with RADIUS, the attributes that came back in the Access-Accept were never passed to the DHCP server, so the DHCP server could not use them when choosing an address and other settings for the client.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds a RADIUS Attributes suboption, suboption code 7, to the DHCP Relay Agent Information option. The relay agent copies the attributes it received into it and the DHCP server reads them when selecting configuration for the client.
tldr.outcome: The DHCP server can now select a pool based on the RADIUS authorization. The memo limits interoperability to a single administrative domain and was later updated by RFC 9445.

today: RFC 4014 was published in February 2005 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9445. The suboption it defines is still the way a RADIUS decision is carried from the access device to the DHCP server.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
The RADIUS Attributes suboption for the DHCP Relay Agent option provides a way in which a NAS can pass attributes obtained from a RADIUS server to a DHCP server. IEEE 802.1X is an example of a mechanism through which a NAS, such as a switch or a wireless LAN access point, can authenticate the identity of the user of a device before providing layer 2 network access with RADIUS as the Authentication Service, as specified in RFC 3580.

In IEEE 802.1X authenticated access, a device must first exchange some authentication credentials with the NAS. The NAS then supplies these credentials to a RADIUS server, which eventually sends either an Access-Accept or an Access-Reject in response to an Access-Request. The NAS, based on the reply of the RADIUS server, then allows or denies network access to the requesting device.

The access device acts as an IEEE 802.1X Authenticator and adds a DHCP relay agent option that includes a RADIUS Attributes suboption to DHCP messages. At the successful conclusion of IEEE 802.1X authentication, a RADIUS Access-Accept provides attributes for service authorizations to the NAS. The NAS stores these attributes locally. When the NAS subsequently relays DHCP messages from the network device, the NAS adds these attributes in a RADIUS Attributes suboption. The RADIUS Attributes suboption is another suboption of the Relay Agent Information option defined in RFC 3046.

The suboption is not limited to use in conjunction with IEEE 802.1X, and can be used to carry RADIUS attributes obtained by the relay agent for any reason. The option is constrained by RADIUS semantics, as set out in section 4 of this document.

The scope of applicability of this specification is such that robust interoperability is only guaranteed for RADIUS service implementations that exist within the same scope as does the DHCP service implementation, that is, within a single, localized administrative domain. Global interoperability of this specification, across administrative domains, is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the access device keeps the RADIUS answer to itself and the DHCP server never hears about it. This document connects the two, so the DHCP server can take the RADIUS decision into account. It only aims to work inside one administrative domain.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The DHCP terms used are the DHCP relay agent, the DHCP server and the DHCP client, as defined in RFC 2131 and RFC 3046.

The RADIUS terms are used in conjunction with RADIUS. A RADIUS server is responsible for receiving user connection requests, authenticating the user, and then returning all configuration information necessary for the client to deliver service to the user. An Attribute is a Type-Length-Value tuple encapsulating data elements as defined in RFC 2865. A Network Access Server, or NAS, provides access to the network and operates as a client of RADIUS. The client is responsible for passing user information to designated RADIUS servers and then acting on the response that is returned. Unlike a traditional dial NAS, the NAS considered here may not have a protocol such as PPP through which it can pass configuration information from the RADIUS attributes to the client.

The IEEE 802.1X terms used are Authenticator and Supplicant, as defined in the IEEE 802.1X protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The key terms are the RADIUS server, which decides who is allowed in, the NAS, which is the device asking the RADIUS server on the user's behalf, and the Attribute, which is one labelled piece of information in a RADIUS message.

sections.title: The RADIUS Attributes Suboption Format
sections.content:
The RADIUS Attributes suboption is a new suboption for the DHCP Relay Agent option. Its format is a one-octet suboption code, a one-octet length N, and then the RADIUS attributes in octets o1 through oN. The RADIUS attributes are encoded according to the encoding rules in RFC 2865. The DHCP relay agent truncates the RADIUS attributes to fit in the RADIUS Attributes suboption.

IANA has assigned the value of 7 for the DHCP Relay Agent Information option suboption code for this suboption.
sections.plainLanguage: The suboption is a code, a length, and then the RADIUS attributes copied straight into it. If they do not fit, the relay agent cuts them short.

sections.title: DHCP Relay Agent Behavior
sections.content:
When the DHCP relay agent receives a DHCP message from the client, it MAY append a DHCP Relay Agent Information option containing the RADIUS Attributes suboption, along with any other suboptions it is configured to supply. The RADIUS Attributes suboption MUST only contain the attributes provided in the RADIUS Access-Accept message, and the DHCP relay agent MUST NOT add more than one RADIUS Attributes suboption in a message.

The relay agent MUST include the User-Name and Framed-Pool attributes in the RADIUS Attributes suboption if they are available, and MAY include other attributes.

To avoid dependencies between the address allocation and other state information between the RADIUS server and the DHCP server, the DHCP relay agent SHOULD include only the attributes in the table below in an instance of the RADIUS Attributes suboption. The table, based on the analysis in RFC 3580, lists attributes that MAY be included: User-Name, Service-Type, Vendor-Specific, Session-Timeout, Framed-Pool and Framed-IPv6-Pool.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay agent copies across only what the RADIUS server actually sent in the Access-Accept, and it may send at most one such suboption per message. It must include the user name and the pool when the server supplied them.

sections.title: DHCP Server Behavior
sections.content: When the DHCP server receives a message from a relay agent containing a RADIUS Attributes suboption, it extracts the contents of the suboption and uses that information in selecting configuration parameters for the client. If the relay agent relays RADIUS attributes that are not included in the table in section 4, the DHCP server SHOULD ignore them. If the DHCP server uses attributes not specified here, it might result in side effects not anticipated in the existing RADIUS specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The DHCP server takes the attributes out of the suboption and uses them when choosing the client's settings. Attributes outside the listed set should be ignored, because acting on them could cause side effects nobody planned for.

sections.title: DHCP Client Behavior
sections.content: Relay agent options are exchanged only between relay agents and the DHCP server, so DHCP clients are never aware of their use.
sections.plainLanguage: The client never sees this. The suboption travels between the relay agent and the DHCP server only.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Message authentication in DHCP for intradomain use, where the out-of-band exchange of a shared secret is feasible, is defined in RFC 3118. Potential exposures to attack are discussed in section 7 of the DHCP protocol specification in RFC 2131.

The DHCP Relay Agent option depends on a trusted relationship between the DHCP relay agent and the server, as described in section 5 of RFC 3046. Although the introduction of fraudulent relay-agent options can be prevented by a perimeter defense that blocks these options unless the relay agent is trusted, a deeper defense using the authentication option for relay agent options or IPsec SHOULD be deployed as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can inject a relay agent option can influence what address a client gets, so the link between the relay agent and the DHCP server has to be protected, not just the edge of the network.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned the value of 7 for the DHCP Relay Agent Information option suboption code for this suboption. This document does not define any new namespaces or other constants for which IANA must maintain a registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The only registration needed is the number 7 for the suboption code. Nothing else was added.
